title: Enhance search with vector embeddings and Amazon OpenSearch Service
key_points: Business-level case for adding vector embeddings to keyword search in OpenSearch, with examples from Prime Video, Amazon Music and Juicebox.
First of a series; no build steps, and search relevance is off the reader's path.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service
authors: Prashant Agrawal, Jon Handler, Ronil Prasad

title: Scaling cluster manager and admin APIs in Amazon OpenSearch Service
key_points: Engineering write-up of how OpenSearch Service changed cluster-state handling and admin APIs (local aggregation, request cancellation, pagination) so very large clusters stay stable under monitoring traffic.
Internal engine detail for OpenSearch operators.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service
authors: Rajiv Kumar Vaidyanathan, Shweta Thareja

title: Optimize Amazon EMR runtime for Apache Spark with EMR S3A
key_points: In current EMR releases an AWS-improved S3A connector replaces EMRFS as the default S3 file system on every EMR deployment option, keeping open-source Spark API compatibility.
AWS reports TPC-DS 3 TB reads on par with EMRFS and slightly faster than open-source S3A, while dynamic partition overwrite ran about 3x faster than EMRFS and far faster than open-source S3A.
No action needed beyond upgrading; the gain shows up mostly in partition-overwrite style writes.
services: Amazon EMR, Apache Spark, Amazon S3
decision: EMRFS vs EMR S3A vs open-source S3A as the Spark S3 connector, mainly for partition-overwrite writes
authors: Giovanni Matteo Fumarola, Narayanan Venkateswaran, Syed Shameerur Rahman, Sushil Kumar Shivashankar, Rajarshi Sarkar

title: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless monitoring: A CloudWatch setup guide
key_points: Lists the CloudWatch metrics that matter for OpenSearch Serverless collections, suggested alarm thresholds, and how to create alarms via console, CLI or CloudFormation, plus a dashboard.
Operational checklist for a service the reader does not run.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, Amazon CloudWatch, AWS CloudFormation
authors: Urmila Iyer, Parth Shah

title: Accelerating SQL analytics with Amazon Redshift MCP server
key_points: AWS's open-source Redshift MCP server lets an AI assistant (Q CLI, Claude Desktop, Kiro or any MCP client) discover provisioned clusters and Serverless workgroups, browse schemas and run queries through the Data API.
Queries run read-only by default, needing only a short list of describe and Data API permissions; the walkthrough explores purchase data and compares figures across two clusters in plain language.
Quick to try against an existing Serverless workgroup; the open question is how often the generated SQL is actually right, which the post leaves to the user to verify.
services: Amazon Redshift, Redshift Serverless, Redshift Data API, Model Context Protocol, Amazon Q Developer
decision: Read-only MCP server vs hand-written SQL vs custom text-to-SQL app for letting AI assistants query the warehouse
attaches_to: dbt-pipelines (Redshift Serverless, NYC 311 marts); aws-bytes: GenAI on data (later)
authors: Ramkumar Nottath, Rohit Vashishtha

title: Use Apache Airflow workflows to orchestrate data processing on Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio
key_points: Shows the code-first side of SageMaker Unified Studio workflows: Airflow DAGs (running on MWAA) that chain notebooks for ingesting and joining weather and taxi data, then train and score a fare model.
Covers authoring, testing and monitoring DAGs inside the studio; the pipeline itself is a simple sequence.
Mainly useful as a view of how Airflow is embedded in SageMaker rather than as orchestration design.
services: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, Amazon MWAA, Apache Airflow, Amazon SageMaker AI
decision: Code-first Airflow DAGs vs visual workflow builder for orchestrating notebook-based pipelines in SageMaker Unified Studio
authors: Vinod Jayendra, Kamen Sharlandjiev, Sean Bjurstrom, Suba Palanisamy

title: Trellix achieved 35% cost savings and enhanced security with Amazon OpenSearch Service
key_points: Trellix moved security-log analytics from self-managed Elasticsearch on EC2 to OpenSearch Service, fed by S3 events through SNS and SQS into OpenSearch Ingestion, with index lifecycle policies moving data across tiers.
AWS reports a 35% cut in storage cost from tiering and tighter retention.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service, Amazon OpenSearch Ingestion, Amazon S3, Amazon SNS, Amazon SQS
authors: Trellix — Leeneksh Dubey, Harsh Bansal, Prashant Agrawal

title: Announcing cross-account ingestion for Amazon OpenSearch Service
key_points: OpenSearch Ingestion pipelines with push sources (HTTP, OpenTelemetry) can be shared with other accounts through a resource policy and pipeline endpoints, instead of VPC peering or Transit Gateway.
Useful for central observability teams; outside the reader's data-pipeline work.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Ingestion, Amazon OpenSearch Service
authors: David Venable

title: Integrate Tableau and PingFederate with Amazon Redshift using AWS IAM Identity Center
key_points: Long setup guide for single sign-on from Tableau to Redshift: PingFederate syncs users to IAM Identity Center via SAML and SCIM, and a trusted token issuer handles the OIDC exchange for the external client.
Identity administration for one specific IdP and BI tool rather than data engineering.
services: Amazon Redshift, AWS IAM Identity Center, PingFederate, Tableau
authors: Rohit Vashishtha, Jared Warren, Jason Veinot, Maneesh Sharma

title: Unlock the power of Apache Iceberg v3 deletion vectors on Amazon EMR
key_points: Iceberg v3 replaces v2's positional delete files with one compressed deletion vector per data file stored in Puffin files, so merge-on-read tables accumulate fewer small delete files and reads merge less.
AWS reports that on a small test table in EMR 7.10, v3 deletes ran about 55% faster, full reads about 28% faster and the delete file was about 74% smaller than with v2.
The test is toy-scale and, at publication, Spark was the only engine supporting deletion vectors, so the gain at realistic update volumes and engine coverage are still open questions worth measuring.
services: Apache Iceberg, Amazon EMR, Apache Spark, AWS Glue Data Catalog, Amazon S3
decision: Iceberg v2 positional deletes vs v3 deletion vectors vs copy-on-write for update-heavy tables
attaches_to: aws-bytes: File Layout Optimization (active); dbt-pipelines (Iceberg folder)
authors: Arun Shanmugam, Kinshuk Pahare, Linda O'Connor, Suthan Phillips

title: Tailor Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio project environments to your needs using custom blueprints
key_points: Admins can now define custom CloudFormation-based blueprints for SageMaker Unified Studio projects, including their own managed IAM policies on the project role.
Platform-admin setup steps; little for a data engineer outside a SageMaker rollout.
services: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, AWS CloudFormation, AWS IAM
authors: Aditya Challa, Khushbu Agarwal

title: Get started with Amazon OpenSearch Service: T-shirt size your domain for log analytics
key_points: Gives small/medium/large starting configurations for OpenSearch log-analytics domains, deriving shard counts, instance types and node counts from daily volume and retention.
Assumes time-based daily indexes with replicas spread across zones; OpenSearch capacity planning only.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service
authors: Harsh Bansal, Aditya Challa, Raaga N.G

title: Amazon SageMaker introduces Amazon S3 based shared storage for enhanced project collaboration
key_points: New SageMaker Unified Studio projects store shared files in a project S3 prefix by default, replacing CodeCommit, with Git still available for version control.
Shared files are visible across JupyterLab, the query editor and visual ETL; a workspace-convenience change.
services: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, Amazon S3
authors: Hari Ramesh, Anagha Barve, Anchit Gupta, Saurabh Bhutyani, Zach Mitchell

title: Streamline Spark application development on Amazon EMR with the Data Solutions Framework on AWS
key_points: Uses the open-source Data Solutions Framework (CDK constructs) to package a PySpark app with its EMR Serverless infrastructure in one repository, developed and tested locally first.
A self-updating CDK pipeline deploys to staging and production accounts and runs an integration test job before promotion.
Shows a developer-owned path from code to deployed Spark job without a separate platform team.
services: Amazon EMR, Amazon EMR Serverless, AWS CDK, Data Solutions Framework on AWS, AWS CodePipeline
decision: Developer-owned CDK app with infra and CI/CD vs separate platform-team infrastructure for deploying Spark jobs
authors: Vincent Gromakowski, Jan Michael Go Tan, Lotfi Mouhib

title: Break down data silos and seamlessly query Iceberg tables in Amazon SageMaker from Snowflake
key_points: Snowflake reads Iceberg tables that live in S3 and are registered in the Glue Data Catalog by calling Glue's Iceberg REST endpoint, with Lake Formation deciding what Snowflake's IAM role may see.
Setup: an IAM role for Snowflake, Lake Formation grants and S3 location registration, then a catalog integration in Snowflake; catalog-linked databases pick up new tables and changes automatically.
The reverse direction of the later Samsung Ads pattern: AWS keeps the catalog and the data, another engine queries it with no copy.
services: AWS Glue Data Catalog, AWS Lake Formation, Apache Iceberg, Amazon S3, Amazon SageMaker Lakehouse, Snowflake
decision: Expose the Glue catalog to Snowflake over Iceberg REST vs copy data into Snowflake vs federate Snowflake's catalog into AWS
authors: Snowflake — Nidhi Gupta, Andries Engelbrecht

title: Automate and orchestrate Amazon EMR jobs using AWS Step Functions and Amazon EventBridge
key_points: An EventBridge schedule starts a Step Functions workflow that creates a transient EMR on EC2 cluster, submits a PySpark step, waits for it and always terminates the cluster, deployed from a CloudFormation template.
Aimed at teams that need EC2-level control for compliance; covers monitoring through Step Functions, EMR step status and CloudWatch logs.
A standard pattern; where that control is not needed, EMR Serverless or Glue removes the cluster lifecycle entirely.
services: AWS Step Functions, Amazon EMR, Amazon EventBridge, Amazon CloudWatch, AWS CloudFormation
decision: Transient EMR on EC2 orchestrated by Step Functions vs EMR Serverless vs Glue for scheduled Spark batch jobs
authors: Senthil Kamala Rathinam, Shashidhar Makkapati

title: Accelerate your data and AI workflows by connecting to Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio from Visual Studio Code
key_points: A local VS Code can open SageMaker Unified Studio spaces remotely through the AWS Toolkit and Systems Manager, keeping personal IDE settings while running on project compute.
Developer-experience setup, plus how admins can turn remote access off.
services: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, AWS Toolkit for VS Code, AWS Systems Manager
authors: Lauren Mullennex, Anagha Barve, Anchit Gupta, Bhargava Varadharajan

title: Use the Amazon DataZone upgrade domain to Amazon SageMaker and expand to new SQL analytics, data processing, and AI uses cases
key_points: Existing DataZone domains can be upgraded to SageMaker Unified Studio while keeping assets, metadata forms, glossaries and subscriptions, and both portals stay available during rollout.
Short announcement aimed at existing DataZone customers; the reader has no DataZone footprint to upgrade.
services: Amazon DataZone, Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio
authors: David Victoria, Leonardo Gomez

title: Migrating from API keys to service account tokens in Grafana dashboards using Terraform
key_points: Replaces Amazon Managed Grafana API keys with service-account tokens for automation, stored in Secrets Manager and rotated by Lambda, all provisioned with Terraform.
Credential housekeeping for a dashboarding tool; unrelated to data pipelines.
services: Amazon Managed Grafana, AWS Secrets Manager, AWS Lambda, Terraform
authors: Majdoulina Makbal

title: Build a streaming data mesh using Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
key_points: Applies data-mesh roles to streaming: producers own and evolve the stream as a product, consumers read it on their own terms, and a governance team runs capacity, retention, encryption and access.

Three access patterns built on Kinesis: shared reads with replay (standard or enhanced fan-out, long retention), rule-based filtering via Lambda event-source-mapping filters, and replay-free fan-out to web clients through AppSync or API Gateway WebSockets.

Practical sharing details: resource policies or cross-account roles, tag-based access control, Glue Schema Registry for schemas, and the catch that the KPL cannot write to a stream in another account.
services: Amazon Kinesis, Kinesis Data Streams, AWS Lambda, AWS Glue Schema Registry, AWS AppSync, Amazon API Gateway, AWS IAM
decision: Shared stream with replay vs filtered consumer vs replay-free fan-out for sharing streaming data across teams and accounts
authors: Felix John, Ali Alemi

title: Decrease your storage costs with Amazon OpenSearch Service index rollups
key_points: OpenSearch index rollups summarise old time-series log data into coarser indexes, so history stays queryable at lower storage cost in any tier.
Covers schema choices, creating and monitoring rollup jobs, and automating them with Index State Management policies; OpenSearch log-analytics tuning.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service
authors: Luis Tiani, Muhammad Ali, Srikanth Daggumalli

title: Introducing restricted classification terms for governed classification in Amazon SageMaker Catalog
key_points: SageMaker Catalog glossaries can now be marked restricted, so only authorised users or groups may tag assets with sensitive classifications such as PHI or PCI.
Matters because those tags can drive downstream automation like automatic access grants, so a wrongly applied tag is a governance risk, not just bad metadata.
services: Amazon SageMaker Catalog, Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio
decision: Open glossary tagging vs restricted classification terms for sensitive-data labels that drive access
authors: Ramesh H Singh, Abbas Makhdum, Mohit Dawar, Pradeep Misra

title: Introducing enhanced AI assistance in Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio: Agentic chat, Amazon Q Developer CLI, and MCP integration
key_points: Q Developer chat and CLI inside SageMaker Unified Studio's IDEs gain project awareness through MCP, so they can read files, run commands, fix notebook errors and draft ETL or ML code against the project's data and compute.
A product walkthrough of one assistant inside one IDE; general coding agents with MCP servers have since covered the same ground.
services: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, Amazon Q Developer, Model Context Protocol
authors: Lauren Mullennex, Siddharth Gupta, Ishneet Kaur, Mohan Gandhi, Mukul Prasad, Murali Balakrishnan Narayanaswamy, Necibe Ahat, Vipin Mohan

title: Announcing SageMaker Unified Studio Workshops for Financial Services
key_points: Announces a set of financial-services workshops for SageMaker Unified Studio and lists their themes.
Pointer to training material only, no technical content.
services: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio
authors: Sanjay Ohri, Raghu Prabhu

title: Accelerate AWS Glue zero-ETL data ingestion using Salesforce Bulk API
key_points: Glue zero-ETL from Salesforce now uses the Bulk API by default and falls back to the REST API only for compound fields such as addresses, which the Bulk API cannot return.
AWS reports a 10-million-record custom object loaded in about 6 minutes instead of about 29 with the REST API, and wide objects of several hundred columns loading in around 2 minutes.
Nothing to configure: existing integrations pick it up, so the value is knowing that API quotas and wide objects are less of a blocker for zero-ETL into the lakehouse or Redshift.
services: AWS Glue, Zero-ETL, Salesforce, Amazon Redshift, Amazon SageMaker Lakehouse
decision: Managed zero-ETL vs Glue job with the Salesforce connector vs third-party tool for bulk Salesforce ingestion
authors: Shashank Sharma, Shashi Shekhar

title: Achieve full control over your data encryption using customer managed keys in Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink
key_points: Managed Flink can now encrypt checkpoints, snapshots and running state with a customer-managed KMS key instead of an AWS-owned one.
Most of the post is key-policy and operator-permission sequencing, key rotation, and the gotcha that a new key only applies after a restart; compliance plumbing for regulated teams.
services: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, AWS KMS, AWS CloudFormation
authors: Lorenzo Nicora, Sofie Zilberman

title: Deep dive into the Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink application lifecycle – Part 2
key_points: Covers what goes wrong in practice: an unhandled error puts Flink into a fail-and-restart loop from the last checkpoint, and a bad deploy can leave the application stuck while starting or updating.
Recovery options are an explicit rollback, an update back to the previous configuration, or a force-stop; each has different consequences for state.
Monitoring advice: alert on the full-restarts metric to catch restart loops, and check application, job and subtask status separately because the application can look running while the job is not.
services: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, Apache Flink, Amazon CloudWatch
decision: Rollback vs re-deploy previous config vs force-stop when a stateful Flink deployment fails
authors: Lorenzo Nicora, Felix John

title: Deep dive into the Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink application lifecycle – Part 1
key_points: Explains what the managed Flink service actually does on each API call (create, start, update, stop, start from a snapshot) so that CI/CD or IaC automation around it can be written with the right expectations.
Walks through how a job manager and task managers are brought up on start and how state is restored from a snapshot, which explains why updates restart the job.
Covers the happy path only; the follow-up post covers failures and monitoring.
services: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, Apache Flink
decision: Console/manual operations vs API-driven CI/CD automation for deploying and updating stateful Flink applications
authors: Lorenzo Nicora, Felix John

title: Use account-agnostic, reusable project profiles in Amazon SageMaker to streamline governance
key_points: SageMaker Unified Studio project profiles no longer have to name an account and Region up front; they point at an account pool and the target is chosen when a project is created.
Admin walkthrough for creating pools and assigning them to profiles; platform administration, not data work.
services: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, Amazon DataZone
authors: Ramesh H Singh, Brian Ross, Nira Jaiswal, Somdeb Bhattacharjee

title: Deploy Apache YuniKorn batch scheduler for Amazon EMR on EKS
key_points: Swaps the default Kubernetes scheduler for Apache YuniKorn on EMR on EKS so Spark drivers and executors are placed together (gang scheduling), with hierarchical queues, quotas and priorities per team.
Mostly EKS and Helm setup plus demo scenarios showing queued jobs no longer half-starting; a Kubernetes platform concern rather than data engineering.
services: Amazon EMR, Amazon EMR on EKS, Amazon EKS, Apache YuniKorn
authors: Suvojit Dasgupta, Greg Fina, Matt Poland, Peter Manastyrny
